stops.name: Buenos Aires — Viaje olvidado published
stops.campa: Sur, her own sister's press, publishes Silvina's first book: twenty-eight stories of circus performers, governesses, sick children, and unswervingly loyal servants, drawn from the same nurseries and service quarters of her own childhood. It passes almost unnoticed. Borges, reading her prose for the first time as a body of work, will later name the trait in it that unsettles him most: a strange love for an innocent, or oblique, cruelty he cannot quite account for.
stops.quote: Hay un rasgo que aún no he llegado a comprender bien: cierto extraño amor por la crueldad inocente, o si se quiere, oblicua.
stops.quote_source: Jorge Luis Borges, on the prose of Silvina Ocampo

stops.name: Las Flores — the marriage to Bioy Casares
stops.campa: After six years together at Rincón Viejo, Silvina and Adolfo marry at the civil registry of Las Flores, Borges among the witnesses alongside Óscar Pardo and Enrique Drago Mitre. There is no party, no celebration, little more than a formality after so long an informal life; she is thirty-six, he twenty-five. The marriage that follows will run more than fifty years, unconventional to the end, each of them keeping rooms, hours, and, in his case, other loves the other learns to hold at a private distance.

stops.name: Buenos Aires — Antología de la literatura fantástica published
stops.campa: Silvina, Borges, and Bioy Casares publish together, through Sudamericana, an anthology of fantastic tales gathered from ancient China to contemporary England and France — Kafka, Chesterton, Cocteau, Dunany, Poe among them. Bioy signs the modest prologue for all three. It is the first time the three names appear bound together on a title page, an emblem of the alliance of taste and friendship that will outlast, in print, nearly everything else that happens to any of them.
stops.quote: Este volumen es, simplemente, la reunión de los textos de la literatura fantástica que nos parecen mejores.
stops.quote_source: Adolfo Bioy Casares, prólogo to Antología de la literatura fantástica (1940)

stops.name: Buenos Aires — Enumeración de la patria, Borges' review
stops.campa: Her first book of poems recovers the old Castilian meters to enumerate the rivers, saints' days, and cattle-land of Argentina itself, the country of her own family's estancias turned into verse. Borges reviews it in Sur, comparing the new poet to Whitman, the first public crowning of Silvina as a writer in her own right rather than merely someone's sister, someone's friend, and soon, someone's wife.

stops.name: Buenos Aires — Espacios métricos and the Premio Municipal
stops.campa: A second collection of verse, its very title borrowed from the language of geometry she learned from Léger, measures stanzas the way she once measured a canvas. It wins the Premio Municipal de Poesía, the city of Buenos Aires formally recognizing what her family and her closest readers already knew: whatever else she is, she is now, undeniably, a poet.

stops.name: Mar del Plata — writing Los que aman, odian with Bioy
stops.campa: At the end of summer, by the sea, Silvina and Adolfo write a detective novel together in a little over a month, inventing episodes between them and recognizing at once, without argument, which sentence is the right one. It becomes Los que aman, odian, a poisoning at a solitary beach hotel, the only novel the two of them will ever sign jointly — proof, Bioy will say, that Silvina's originality was inevitable and that working beside her was nothing but a pleasure.
stops.quote: Nunca hubo una discusión ni una pelea con Silvina: inventábamos episodios, alguien proponía una solución y yo escribía... la aceptábamos sin discusiones.
stops.quote_source: Adolfo Bioy Casares, on writing Los que aman, odian (1946)

stops.name: Buenos Aires — Autobiografía de Irene published
stops.campa: Five stories, the title piece narrated by Irene Andrade, a young woman cursed to see the future while she forgets the past entirely — memory itself doubled and inverted, the fantastic turned inward as a psychological condition rather than an external marvel. It is the clearest early statement of the device Silvina will use for the rest of her career: the uncanny not as intrusion from outside but as the ordinary shape of a mind examining itself.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Posadas 1650 — Marta, the given daughter
stops.campa: In the United States, one of Bioy's lovers gives birth to his daughter, Marta. Silvina, fifty and childless, receives the infant into the marriage at the family's Recoleta apartment and adopts her formally as her own, overprotecting the girl for the rest of her life. It is a private act of grief and generosity the public Sur circle rarely mentions, hidden the way most of the real weather of this marriage stays hidden behind its literary partnership.

stops.name: Buenos Aires — La furia published
stops.campa: The collection critics later call the one that ferociously inaugurates her true narrative voice: a golden hare, a jealousy monologue turning in on itself without end, ordinary households harboring an evil no one names directly. The oblique cruelty Borges noticed in her first book, twenty years earlier, is now fully unsheathed, deliberate, and entirely her own instrument.

stops.name: Buenos Aires — Las invitadas published
stops.campa: Thirty stories of women and girls, small thefts of identity, guests who never quite belong in the houses that contain them. Reviewers will later read the title as a private joke: Silvina herself has spent thirty years being introduced in other people's houses as somebody's sister, somebody's wife, somebody's friend, never quite at home under her own name.

stops.name: Buenos Aires — Alejandra Pizarnik at Sara Facio's studio
stops.campa: At the photographer Sara Facio's studio, the young poet Alejandra Pizarnik, sitting for a portrait, loses the composed persona she has built the instant Silvina walks into the room. Over the years that follow Pizarnik writes her six letters of admiration, confidence, and increasingly desperate affection, calling her a lost paradise; Silvina answers with the same careful, unhurried reserve she gives everyone, a kindness that will not, in the end, be quite enough.
stops.quote_source: Alejandra Pizarnik, letter to Silvina Ocampo, c. 1969-1972 (published correspondence)

stops.name: Buenos Aires — Lo amargo por dulce published
stops.campa: A book of poems whose title turns a proverb inside out, bitterness disguised as sweetness — the same device she has used in prose for twenty-five years now given fully to verse: nursery rhyme meters carrying an adult's dread, comfort words holding something that does not comfort at all. Critics reaching for her in this decade still default to describing her as Bioy's wife or Borges's friend; the poems themselves, read closely, answer that condescension by refusing every consoling cliché of domestic verse from the inside.
